hook_text: The oxidising agent gets REDUCED. Sounds backwards. It isn't — and one pickpocket explains why.
clip_script: Drop a strip of grey zinc into blue copper solution and watch: the strip grows a copper coat, and the blue slowly drains out of the water. What you're watching is a robbery. Every atom keeps an electron account, and chemists audit the books with things called oxidation numbers. The audit says: zinc went from zero to plus two — it PAID two electrons. Copper ions went from plus two to zero — they COLLECTED them. Losing electrons is oxidation, gaining is reduction. OIL RIG. Now the naming that trips everyone at exam time: the copper ion — the taker — is called the OXIDISING agent, and it ends up reduced. Backwards? No. Agents are named for what they do to the OTHER guy. The pickpocket is named by the victim's loss. Copper caused zinc's oxidation, so copper is the oxidising agent — and taking electrons means getting reduced yourself. Say it until it's boring: oxidising agent gets reduced, reducing agent gets oxidised. And here's why this topic matters: run that electron payment through a wire instead of a beaker, and you've built a battery. That's Grade 12. This robbery is the rehearsal.
visual_style: Macro shot of a zinc strip furring over with copper as blue fades from the liquid; electron coins visibly hopping from zinc's account ledger to copper's; a cheeky pickpocket silhouette naming beat; end on the beaker morphing into a battery.
mood: True-crime playful — a chemical robbery narrated like a heist.
pacing: Slow visual open on the colour change, quick ledger beats, the naming twist, battery punchline.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and balance any redox equation in four steps.
